messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bus Driver
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Auditory (Sounds): Related sounds
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Michael was 53, a married bus driver who had spent most of his adult life in the routine of early starts, long routes, and the steady responsibility of carrying other people safely where they needed to go. He had not come to treatment for the first time lightly; for months he had told himself he could manage on his own, that he should be able to put the past behind him, and that there was no point in revisiting something so degrading. But the same event that had once split his sense of safety into before and after continued to intrude in ways that made ordinary workdays feel unrecognizable.

The rape had happened in a situation where he had believed he was simply vulnerable, not in danger. Michael described being overpowered and left with the sense that his body had been taken from him while he was unable to stop it. What stayed with him most was not only what happened, but the helpless terror of it, the knowledge that he had been trapped and that no amount of willing himself to fight back had made a difference. In the weeks afterward, he found that remembering it did not feel like recalling something safely in the past. When it came into his mind, the terror returned in full force, as if his body had not understood that the danger was over. He would catch himself in the middle of the day and be struck by a wave of the same panic he had felt then, his chest tightening before he even had words for what was happening.

He also carried a deep shame about the assault, a shame that settled over him every time the memory surfaced. Michael said that what happened had changed how he experienced his own body, and that this was one of the hardest parts to put into words. He felt marked by it. Even years later, he could become overwhelmed by disgust and humiliation at the thought of what had been done to him, and there were moments when he seemed almost unable to bear his own recollection. Rather than forming a clear story in his mind, the event returned as if it were being projected at him. He described the memory as a film that played over and over, repeating the same scenes with the same force, whether he wanted them or not. At times he would be talking to his wife and suddenly lose track of the conversation because an image or sensation from that night had started replaying behind his eyes.

The memories were especially likely to break through when he was tired. On long shifts, after several hours behind the wheel, fatigue made him feel less able to keep the images at bay. He noticed that exhaustion left him more exposed to the memory, as though tiredness loosened his grip on the present. Driving with other people was also a marked trigger. Because his job required him to have passengers seated behind him and beside him, he often found himself acutely aware of their presence in the enclosed bus, especially on crowded runs where he could not easily move or get distance. He did not say that anything on the bus was happening to him now, but the situation itself made him uneasy in a way he could not dismiss. Certain sounds were equally potent: related sounds could stop him cold, especially if they resembled elements of the assault enough to pull him back into that moment. A noise in the environment could hook directly into the memory and make it feel immediate again.

Over time, Michael’s view of other people shifted as well. He had come to believe that people could not be trusted, and that belief sat heavily in the background of his daily life. He no longer felt the easy assumption that others were basically safe. He spoke as someone who had lost faith not only in people, but in life more generally and in any higher power that might have been supposed to protect him. The assault had left him feeling that the world could not be relied upon to be fair or even understandable. That loss of trust was not abstract for him; it shaped how he moved through his days, including the way he watched passengers and kept himself emotionally guarded even with those closest to him.

He had also become increasingly ashamed of what had happened to his body, and that shame made him withdraw from any situation where he felt exposed. The consequences were most visible at work and at home. On the bus, he could push through a route, but the experience cost him. He had begun dreading particularly long drives with passengers, and there were times he felt he was simply enduring the shift rather than doing the job he had once taken pride in. At home, he remained married and committed to his wife, but the burden of secrecy and shame left him isolated in a way she could feel without fully understanding.

Michael eventually sought help because the intrusions were wearing him down and he could no longer keep pretending that the memory was behind him. He was tired of feeling ambushed by terror, tired of the replaying images, and tired of carrying the conviction that his body had been violated in a way he could never fully explain to anyone else. What he most feared was that the memories would keep surfacing in the middle of ordinary life and make him feel trapped again; what he most hoped for was some way to get through a day on the bus, and at home with his wife, without feeling as though the assault were still happening inside him.
